bodyMarkdown:
## From Hourly to Annual: The 38-Hour Week and the NRL Salary Cap

Understanding how your hourly rate translates into an annual salary is essential whether you are negotiating a pay rise, comparing job offers, or planning your budget. In Australia, the standard full-time working week is 38 hours, as defined by the Fair Work Act. This article explains the conversion formula, highlights the national minimum wage, award rates, casual loading, superannuation, and tax, and contrasts these with the NRL salary cap figures for 2026.

### The Basic Conversion Formula

To estimate your annual gross pay, multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then by 52 weeks. For a full-time employee on 38 hours per week:

**Annual gross ≈ hourly rate × 38 × 52**

For example, if you earn $30 per hour:

$30 × 38 × 52 = $59,280 per year

Your fortnightly pay would be roughly $2,280 (weekly × 2). This formula assumes you work the same hours every week with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. For a more personalised calculation, use [the timesheet](/).

### The National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

The Fair Work Commission sets the national minimum wage each year. From 1 July 2026, the rate is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. This applies to adult employees not covered by an award or agreement.

Many industries have modern awards that set higher minimum rates for specific roles. For example, the Supported Employment Services Award has its own pay guide. You can find the correct rate for your job using [pay guides](/blog) from the Fair Work Ombudsman.

#### Casual Loading

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base rate. For the national minimum wage, this means $33.05 per hour. The loading compensates for the lack of paid leave entitlements. When using our calculator, check the casual loading box to add 25% to your base hourly rate – do not enter a rate that already includes the loading. Learn more about [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading).

### Superannuation and Tax

Superannuation guarantee contributions are paid by your employer on top of your ordinary earnings. From 1 July 2026, the rate is 12% of your ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. For an employee earning $59,280, the super contribution would be approximately $7,113.60 per year. This is not deducted from your pay; it is an additional benefit. See [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) for more details.

Income tax for 2026–27 uses the resident tax-free threshold of $18,200. The rates are:
- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income between $18,201 and $45,000
- 30% on income between $45,001 and $135,000
- 37% on income between $135,001 and $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

A Medicare levy of 2% generally applies. Our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) estimator can help you see your net income after tax and Medicare.

### Comparing with the NRL Salary Cap

The NRL salary cap provides an interesting benchmark for high earnings in professional sport. According to the NRL’s salary cap page, the base salary cap for the top 30 players in 2026 is $11.55 million per club, with an additional $300,000 veteran and developed player allowance and $100,000 motor vehicle allowance, making a total cap of $11.95 million. The minimum salary for a top-30 player in 2026 is $140,000 per year.

To put that in hourly terms, $140,000 divided by (38 × 52) equals about $70.85 per hour – more than 2.5 times the national minimum wage. However, NRL players often have non-standard working hours and their contracts include bonuses, image rights, and other benefits that are not captured by a simple hourly rate. Players can also earn unlimited amounts from corporate sponsors unrelated to their club, which are excluded from the salary cap.

Most Australians earn far less than an NRL player. The Australian Bureau of Statistics’ Average Weekly Earnings for May 2026 show full-time adult ordinary time earnings of $2,083.70 per week ($108,352.40 annually), while all employees (including part-time) average $1,579.20 per week ($82,118.40 annually). The [average pay](/topics/average-pay) page provides more context.

### Award Rates and Enterprise Agreements

If you are covered by a modern award, your minimum pay rate will be higher than the national minimum wage. Awards also include penalty rates for weekends, public holidays, and overtime. Enterprise agreements can set different rates, but they must pass the “better off overall” test. The Fair Work Ombudsman’s pay guides list the minimum rates for each award classification. Use [job pay](/topics/job-pay) to find the right award for your industry.

### Important Considerations

The annual figure calculated here is a gross estimate. It does not account for unpaid overtime, salary sacrifice, or deductions such as HELP repayments or the Medicare levy surcharge. Super is paid on top of your ordinary earnings, not deducted from your pay. Always check your specific employment contract and seek professional advice for your personal circumstances.

### Summary

Converting your hourly rate to an annual salary using the 38-hour week gives you a useful starting point for financial planning. The national minimum wage, award rates, and the NRL salary cap illustrate the wide range of earnings in Australia. Use our [reference tables](/data) to compare rates across industries, and remember that your take-home pay will depend on tax, Medicare, and any salary packaging arrangements.
